problems.title: Data race?

options: two threads increment a plain int
two threads read a plain int, nobody writes
one thread writes a plain bool, another spins reading it

hints: Concurrent access, a write, no synchronisation, non-atomic.
problems.solution: Concurrent reads are fine; atomics never race.

problems.title: Deadlock
problems.statement: Thread 1 locks A then B; thread 2 locks B then A.

parts.prompt: Which deadlock condition do you break with a global lock order?

problems.solution: Lock in a consistent order, or let scoped_lock's deadlock-avoidance algorithm do it.

problems.title: Lost increments
problems.statement: Two threads each run for (i = 0; i < 10⁶; ++i) counter++; on a plain int (no sync, no optimisation).

options: anything between about 2 and 2 × 10⁶ (lost updates); and it's UB
per-thread local counters, summed at the end

problems.solution: Local accumulation avoids sharing entirely; atomics work, but bounce the cache line.

options: spurious wakeups / another consumer can empty q: must wait in a loop on the predicate

parts.prompt: If the consumer sees flag == 1, can it print a stale data?

options: Yes, it could see stale data (no ordering)

problems.title: Double-checked locking
problems.solution: The first three establish happens-before; volatile doesn't.

problems.title: Mutex cost
problems.statement: An uncontended lock+unlock ~20 ns; a contended handoff through the kernel ~2 µs.

parts.prompt: What dominates latency in a lock-heavy hot path?

problems.solution: Contention, not the primitive, is the cost. Shrink critical sections, or shard the data.

problems.title: x86 vs ARM
problems.statement: Code with relaxed atomics that "always worked" on x86 fails on ARM.

options: x86 (TSO) orders loads and stores more strongly; ARM reorders, exposing missing acquire/release

problems.solution: Correctness must come from the C++ memory model, not from the hardware you tested on.
